title: Objectives and key results
blurb: Explain what OKRs are, tell an objective from a key result, and know where PRINCE2 Agile teams define them and why.
question: In a PRINCE2 Agile project, what is an OKR, and in which workshop do teams define or update their OKRs?

teach.body: Objectives and key results (OKRs) are a goal-setting framework associated with John Doerr that helps organizations define and track ambitious goals. They help an organization focus on what matters most and align its teams around common goals. In PRINCE2 Agile, OKRs are an artifact of the progress practice: they give teams a shared target and a measurable way to see whether they are moving towards it.

rows.label: Answers
values: Where do we want to get to?
How will we know we are getting there?

rows.label: Measured?
values: Yes, with a number or target

teach.body: An objective is a clear, aspirational goal: it says what the team wants to achieve and should inspire. Key results are specific, measurable outcomes that show progress towards that objective. Together they link a high-level goal to measurable outcomes. In common practice, which grew from Andy Grove's work at Intel before Doerr spread it, each objective has about three to five key results, and a key result is either met or not met.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.3, Glossary; whatmatters.com (background)

teach.caption: Each key result has a number you can check. 'Build a renewal page' would be a task, not a key result.

teach.body: Teams define or update their OKRs in the release planning workshop, held in managing a stage boundary, both for initiation and for later stages. Its 'OKR definition' topic introduces OKRs and their role in agile projects, linking high-level goals to measurable outcomes, and aims for a clear set of OKRs that guide progress and measure success. Each team defines its own OKRs, working alongside the other teams and the project manager.

teach.caption: Table 13.16. The workshop belongs to managing a stage boundary.

teach.body: Because key results are measurable outcomes, a team can check them as releases land and see whether the value it is delivering moves the needle, not just whether stories are done. Shared objectives also keep several teams pulling in the same direction. OKRs are not a tool for assessing agile maturity: that is the job of agile maturity assessments, built on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability.

Ravensby is building a resident parking permit app with two teams. At the release planning workshop for the next stage, product owner Leah Grant's team sets the objective 'make permit renewal effortless' with three key results: 80% of renewals online, an average renewal under five minutes, and phone queries down 30%. Project manager Martin Achebe checks they fit the project canvas. The team then breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map.

teach.text: OKR definition is a topic of the RELEASE PLANNING workshop (managing a stage boundary), not the team planning workshop or the project initiation workshop's persona definition. A key result must be measurable: 'launch the new page' is a task. And OKRs align and track goals; they do not assess agile maturity.

items: OKRs: a goal-setting framework (John Doerr) to define and track ambitious goals (12.3.2.3).
Objective: clear, aspirational goal. Key result: specific, measurable outcome showing progress.
They help organizations focus on what matters most and align teams around common goals.
Defined or updated in the 'OKR definition' topic of the release planning workshop (Table 13.16).
Each team defines its own OKRs with the other teams and the project manager.
OKRs are not used to assess agile maturity.

summary: You can now explain what OKRs are, tell an objective from a key result, and spot a well-formed key result. You can also say that teams define or update their OKRs in the release planning workshop at a stage boundary.

A.q: In OKRs, what is a key result?
options: A clear, aspirational goal for the team
A specific, measurable outcome showing progress
A user story accepted by the product owner
A risk response agreed for the release
A.why: Key results are specific, measurable outcomes that indicate progress towards achieving the objective (Glossary, 12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: A clear, aspirational goal is the objective.
whyNot.2: Accepted user stories are outputs of delivery, not key results.
whyNot.3: Risk responses belong to the risk practice.

A.q: Which statement BEST describes the purpose of OKRs?
options: To assess the agile maturity of each delivery team
To record the status and version of each product in the plan
To focus on what matters most and align teams on common goals
To estimate the relative size of user stories in the backlog
A.why: OKRs are designed to help organizations focus on what matters most and align their teams around common goals (12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Agile maturity is assessed with agile maturity assessments, not OKRs.
whyNot.1: Product status is recorded in the product register.
whyNot.3: Relative sizing uses techniques such as story points and magic estimation.

A.q: In which workshop do teams define or update their OKRs?
A.why: The release planning workshop includes an 'OKR definition' topic to define or update team OKRs (Table 13.16).

whyNot.1: The team planning workshop refines the product backlog and plans the next iteration.
whyNot.2: The project initiation workshop covers the Agilometer, management approaches, project DoR and DoD and personas.
whyNot.3: The team retrospective reflects on the last iteration: the good, the bad, the learning, team building.

B.q: A team sets the objective 'make online booking the easy choice for patients'. Which is the BEST key result?
options: Hold a user workshop each iteration
Raise online bookings to 70% by release 3
B.why: A key result is a specific, measurable outcome that shows progress towards the objective (Glossary).

whyNot.0: Redesigning a page is a task or output, not a measurable outcome.
whyNot.1: Holding workshops is an activity, not an outcome showing progress.

B.q: In which process is the release planning workshop, where team OKRs are defined, held?
B.why: The release planning workshop (for initiation and for subsequent stages) belongs to managing a stage boundary (13.7.4.1).

whyNot.0: Managing product delivery holds the team planning and team retrospective workshops.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage holds the progress review workshop.
whyNot.3: Directing a project holds the agile enablement workshop.

B.q:
Which two statements about OKRs in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. An objective is a clear, aspirational goal.
2. OKRs are the main tool for assessing agile maturity.
3. Each team defines its own OKRs with other teams and the project manager.
4. OKRs are set once by the board and not changed afterwards.
B.why: An objective is a clear, aspirational goal (1), and teams define their own OKRs in a workshop with other teams and the PM (3) (12.3.2.3, Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: agile maturity assessments do that, not OKRs.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: OKRs do not assess maturity, and they are defined or updated at each release planning workshop.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: teams define or update OKRs at release planning workshops.

C.q: A team updates its OKRs at a stage boundary and then breaks key activities into user stories. Which workshop is this, and which topic covers the OKRs?
C.why: The release planning workshop has an 'OKR definition' topic followed by 'release planning', where activities become user stories and the release map is updated (Table 13.16).

whyNot.1: Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration; it does not define OKRs.
whyNot.2: The team dashboards topic sets up visual team reporting, not OKRs.
whyNot.3: Persona definition identifies key user personas, not OKRs.

C.q: Who is associated with the OKR framework, and what does it help organizations do?
options: Robert Greenleaf; serve their teams as leaders
Mike Cohn; split epics into smaller stories
John Doerr; define and track ambitious goals
John Brothers; track total risk across iterations
C.why: OKR (John Doerr) is a goal-setting framework that helps organizations define and track ambitious goals (12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Robert Greenleaf is associated with servant leadership.
whyNot.1: Mike Cohn is associated with epics breaking down into detailed stories.
whyNot.3: John Brothers is associated with the cumulative risk burn-down chart.

C.q: Why do OKRs help several delivery teams in one PRINCE2 Agile project?
options: They replace the release map for each team
They align teams around common, measurable goals
They set the time tolerance for each iteration
They decide which team owns the project backlog
C.why: OKRs help organizations focus on what matters most and align teams around common goals, with measurable key results (12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: The release map remains the plan; OKRs give goals to plan towards.
whyNot.2: Time has zero tolerance; OKRs do not set tolerances.
whyNot.3: The CPO owns the project backlog; OKRs do not assign ownership.

reteach.title: Training for a half marathon
reteach.question: What is the goal, and how would you know you are on track?

blocks.body: 'Finish my first half marathon feeling strong' is the objective: clear and motivating, but not a number. The key results are the scoreboard: run 10 km without stopping by March, complete three 15 km runs by April, finish in under 2 hours 15. 'Buy new trainers' is a task, not a key result. Objective says where; key results prove you are getting there.

blocks.text: If you cannot put a number or a clear yes or no on it, it is not a key result.

explain.body: A goal-setting framework (John Doerr) that helps organizations define and track ambitious goals, focus on what matters most and align teams (12.3.2.3).

test.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. OKRs are a goal-setting framework that helps organizations define and track [?] goals.
test.why: 12.3.2.3: OKR is a goal-setting framework that helps organizations define and track ambitious goals.

whyNot.1: OKRs can be updated at each release planning workshop; they are not described as fixed goals.
whyNot.2: OKRs align teams around common goals rather than individual ones.
whyNot.3: Key results can measure any outcome, not just financial ones.

explain.body: Objective: clear, aspirational goal. Key result: specific, measurable outcome that indicates progress towards it (Glossary).

test.q: Which is an objective rather than a key result?
options: Cut average call waiting time to 2 minutes
Reach 5,000 active monthly users by the end of stage 2
Make our service the first choice for local renters
test.why: An objective is a clear, aspirational goal; the other options are specific, measurable outcomes, which are key results.

whyNot.0: A 2-minute target is a measurable outcome: a key result.
whyNot.1: 5,000 active users is a measurable outcome: a key result.
whyNot.3: Under 1% failed payments is a measurable outcome: a key result.

explain.body: In the release planning workshop (managing a stage boundary), teams define or update their OKRs, linking high-level goals to measurable outcomes (Table 13.16).

test.q: What is the goal of the 'OKR definition' topic in the release planning workshop?
options: A prioritized product backlog for the next iteration
A clear set of OKRs to guide progress and measure success
A list of key user personas to guide product decisions
An agreed team delegation matrix for key decisions
test.why: Table 13.16: the goal is a clear set of OKRs to guide project progress and measure success.

whyNot.0: Backlog prioritization happens in the team planning workshop.
whyNot.2: Personas are defined in the project initiation workshop.
whyNot.3: The team delegation matrix is a topic of the project kickoff workshop.

explain.body: OKRs track goals and align teams. Agile maturity is assessed separately, through agile maturity assessments based on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (12.4.1).

test.q: A board member asks which tool shows how agile the teams have become. Which is it?
test.why: Agile maturity assessments, based on psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability, show how agile teams have become; OKRs are not used for this (12.4.1, 12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: OKRs align teams and track goals; they are not used to assess agile maturity.
whyNot.2: The release map plans releases and iterations.
whyNot.3: A burn-up shows completed work against scope.
